note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. I have you down as an 89-year-old male here today because of recurrent falls and to review your medicines. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: Well, I keep ending up on the floor. I have fallen three times in the last two months. The last one was four days ago in the bathroom at night.
Family member: I am his daughter and I drove him in. He is on the floor more than he should be, doctor.
Doctor: Did you hit your head when you fell four days ago, or pass out?
Patient: I bumped my left hip on the tub, but no head injury and no passing out. My legs just felt wobbly and I was lightheaded when I stood up.
Doctor: Do you get lightheaded every time you stand?
Patient: Mostly first thing in the morning and when I get up at night to use the bathroom.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath?
Patient: No chest pain and no shortness of breath. My heart flutters sometimes, but that is old news with the atrial fibrillation.
Doctor: Any black stools, blood in the stool, or nosebleeds? I ask because you take a blood thinner.
Patient: No black stools and no nosebleeds. I do bruise on my arms, though.
Doctor: Any trouble speaking, vision changes, or weakness on one side?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Let us go through the pill bottles you brought. Which blood thinner are you on?
Patient: Apixaban. I take 5 mg twice a day.
Family member: Dad, the bottle says 2.5 mg. The cardiologist lowered it last year.
Patient: Oh, you are right. It is 2.5 mg twice a day. I get the numbers mixed up.
Doctor: Good that we checked. What else do you take?
Patient: Amlodipine 10 mg once a day for blood pressure, metoprolol succinate 50 mg once daily for the heart rhythm, tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night for my prostate, and zolpidem 10 mg at bedtime for sleep. I also take diphenhydramine 25 mg at night, the sleeping pill from the drugstore. And acetaminophen when my knees hurt.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Ibuprofen gave me hives years ago. So I stay away from Advil and Aleve.
Doctor: Noted, a documented allergy to ibuprofen with hives, so we will keep you off all NSAIDs, which would also be unsafe with a blood thinner. Today your blood pressure sitting is 138/78, heart rate 64 and irregular, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and temperature 98.2. After standing for three minutes your blood pressure drops to 104/60, heart rate 70, and you feel lightheaded.
Patient: That is exactly the feeling.
Doctor: Your gait is slow and unsteady, you pushed up with your arms to stand, and the timed up and go test took 21 seconds. Your heart is irregularly irregular without a murmur, your lungs are clear, there is no weakness on either side, and your scalp shows no bruising or swelling. The left hip is tender over the greater trochanter, but the leg is not shortened and you can bear weight. The hip X-ray we did here shows no fracture, and the ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate. The labs from your primary doctor last week show creatinine 1.6, hemoglobin 12.9, and sodium 139.
Family member: Is the dizziness from his heart?
Doctor: Mostly it is from his medicines and his blood pressure dropping when he stands. My impression is recurrent falls from orthostatic hypotension, made worse by polypharmacy. He also has atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, chronic kidney disease, and an enlarged prostate. The amlodipine dose is too high for him now. Zolpidem and diphenhydramine are medicines we try to avoid after age 65 because they cause confusion and falls, and tamsulosin can drop the pressure on standing.
Patient: So what do I do?
Doctor: Here is the plan. Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day, which is the right dose for your age and kidney function. Reduce the amlodipine to 5 mg once a day. Stop the diphenhydramine tonight. Cut the zolpidem to 5 mg at bedtime for two weeks and then stop it. Keep the tamsulosin 0.4 mg, but take it after supper. Continue the metoprolol. For knee pain use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, and no ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. I am referring you to home physical therapy for gait and balance training and a home safety visit. Get up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed first, use a night light, and drink fluids through the day. We will repeat a basic metabolic panel and recheck your standing blood pressure with your primary doctor in two weeks. Because you are on a blood thinner, go straight to the emergency department for any fall where you hit your head, or for black stools or new weakness.
Family member: We will do all of that. Thank you.
summary: An 89-year-old male was seen after three falls in two months, the latest four days ago, with lightheadedness on standing and no head injury or passing out. He has atrial fibrillation on apixaban, high blood pressure, chronic kidney disease, an enlarged prostate and an ibuprofen allergy. Standing blood pressure fell to 104/60, his gait was unsteady, and the hip X-ray showed no fracture. The impression is recurrent falls from orthostatic hypotension worsened by polypharmacy. Amlodipine is reduced to 5 mg, diphenhydramine is stopped, zolpidem is tapered, apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day continues, and home physical therapy and a repeat basic metabolic panel are arranged.

Doctor: Hi there. I see you are a 30-year-old female coming in with pelvic pain. What has been going on?
Patient: I have had pain low in my belly for about two years, but the last month it has been worse. It used to be mostly right before and during my period, but now I feel it most days.
Doctor: How bad is it?
Patient: Usually a 5 out of 10, and an 8 during my period. I also have pain with sex and pain when I move my bowels around my period.
Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, and no burning when I pee. No blood in my urine either.
Doctor: Any bleeding between periods, or vomiting?
Patient: No bleeding between periods and no vomiting. I do get nauseated when the pain is bad.
Doctor: Could you be pregnant?
Patient: I took a home test last week and it was negative.
Doctor: What have you tried for the pain?
Patient: My gynecologist put me on norethindrone acetate 5 mg daily four months ago, and it helped a lot. But I ran out about six weeks ago. It costs too much with my insurance and I could not afford the refill, so I just stopped. The pain came back within a couple of weeks. I have been taking ibuprofen 400 mg when it is bad, but it only takes the edge off.
Doctor: I am sorry the cost got in the way. Let me check your numbers and then examine you. Your blood pressure is 118/72, heart rate 84, temperature 98.4, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Your belly is soft with mild tenderness low on both sides, but no rebound and no guarding. On the pelvic exam your uterus is tender and does not move easily, there is tenderness behind the uterus, no mass, no cervical motion tenderness, and no discharge. The urine pregnancy test we did here is negative, and the urinalysis shows no blood, no leukocytes, and no nitrites.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: My impression is chronic pelvic pain, most likely from endometriosis that flared after the hormone treatment stopped. Nothing today points to an infection or an emergency. For the plan, we will restart norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily, and our pharmacist will find a generic discount program so the refill is affordable. Increase the ibuprofen to 600 mg every 6 hours as needed, taken with food. I am also ordering a pelvic ultrasound, and I want you to see your gynecologist within two weeks to talk about longer term options. Come back right away for severe pain, fever, heavy bleeding, or fainting.
Patient: Okay, thank you. I will do that.
summary: A 30-year-old female presented with two years of pelvic pain, worse over the last month, with pain during sex and with bowel movements around her period. She ran out of norethindrone acetate six weeks ago because of cost and the pain returned despite ibuprofen. She had no fever, discharge, burning with urination or bleeding between periods, her urine pregnancy test and urinalysis were negative, and exam showed mild lower abdominal tenderness and a tender uterus with limited mobility. The impression is chronic pelvic pain, most likely endometriosis that flared after the hormone treatment stopped. Norethindrone acetate 5 mg is restarted with pharmacist help on cost, ibuprofen is increased to 600 mg, and a pelvic ultrasound and gynecology follow-up are planned.

Doctor: Hello, I understand you are a 75-year-old female with a sudden, severe headache. Tell me what happened.
Patient: About an hour ago I was making tea, and then bang, the worst headache of my life. It is at the back of my head.
Doctor: Did it build up slowly or hit you all at once?
Patient: All at once, like a thunderclap. I have never had anything like it.
Doctor: Any fall or injury to your head?
Patient: No fall and no hit to the head.
Doctor: Any vomiting, vision changes, weakness, or trouble speaking?
Patient: I feel a little nauseated, but no vomiting. No vision changes, no weakness, and my speech is fine.
Doctor: Any fever or neck stiffness?
Patient: No fever, and my neck feels fine.
Doctor: Do you have any medical problems, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: High blood pressure. I take amlodipine 5 mg every morning, and that is all.
Doctor: Your blood pressure is 176/94, heart rate 82, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 98.1. You are alert and speaking normally. Your pupils are equal and reactive, your face is symmetric, your strength is normal in both arms and legs, and your neck is supple. This is a thunderclap headache, and I need to rule out bleeding around the brain. We are sending you for a CT scan of the head without contrast right now, and then a CT angiogram. If the CT scan is negative, I may need to do a lumbar puncture. I will give you acetaminophen 1000 mg by mouth for the pain, and you will stay on the monitor. I will update you as soon as the scan is back.
Patient: Okay, please hurry.
summary: A 75-year-old female with high blood pressure presented with a sudden, severe headache that began an hour ago, described as the worst of her life and maximal at onset. She has mild nausea but no vomiting, fever, neck stiffness, vision changes, weakness, trouble speaking or head injury. Blood pressure was 176/94 and her neurologic exam was normal. The clinician diagnoses a thunderclap headache and needs to rule out bleeding around the brain. A CT scan of the head without contrast and a CT angiogram are ordered, a lumbar puncture may follow, and acetaminophen is given.

soap.assessment: Thunderclap headache; bleeding around the brain needs to be ruled out. High blood pressure.

CT angiogram

note:
Visit type: Telephone visit (audio only). Verbal consent for a telephone visit was obtained, and the patient was at home in a quiet room.

Reason for visit: Follow-up of Graves disease in a 57-year-old female, six weeks after starting treatment for hyperthyroidism.

History reported by the patient: She was started on methimazole 10 mg once daily at the last visit. She feels somewhat better but still has palpitations, hand tremor, heat intolerance, and difficulty sleeping. She has lost about 8 pounds over the past two months. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, sore throat, eye pain, double vision, and diarrhea. She denies rash, itching, and yellowing of the skin since starting the methimazole. She has no new neck swelling and no trouble swallowing. She has been taking the methimazole every day without missed doses and has no other chronic medical problems.

Home measurements reported during the call: Blood pressure 138/82 and pulse 104 on her home cuff, and home weight 142 pounds.

Exam: Because this was a telephone visit, no visual or physical examination was possible. Her speech is clear and she speaks in full sentences without audible shortness of breath.

Results reviewed: Labs drawn last week show TSH less than 0.01, free T4 elevated at 3.1, white blood cell count 6.2, and normal liver enzymes.

Impression: Graves disease with persistent hyperthyroidism and symptomatic tachycardia, only partially controlled on methimazole 10 mg once daily. No symptoms to suggest a reaction to methimazole.

Plan: Increase methimazole to 20 mg once daily. Start propranolol 20 mg three times daily for the palpitations and tremor. Counseled to stop methimazole and call the same day for fever, sore throat, rash, or yellowing of the skin. Repeat TSH, free T4, total T3, CBC with differential, and liver panel in 4 weeks, and hold any biotin supplement for several days before the draw. Referral for a baseline eye examination. Telephone follow-up in 4 to 6 weeks after the repeat labs. The patient verbalized understanding and agreed with the plan.
summary: A 57-year-old female with Graves disease was seen by telephone, six weeks into treatment for hyperthyroidism, with persistent palpitations, hand tremor, heat intolerance, difficulty sleeping and about 8 pounds of weight loss. She denies chest pain, fever, sore throat, eye symptoms, rash and yellowing of the skin, and her home pulse was 104 with blood pressure 138/82. Recent labs show TSH below 0.01 and an elevated free T4. The impression is Graves disease with persistent hyperthyroidism and symptomatic tachycardia, only partially controlled on methimazole. Methimazole is increased to 20 mg once daily, propranolol is started, repeat labs are ordered for 4 weeks, and an eye examination referral is made.

note:
51 yo M seen at urgent care. Hx RA on methotrexate (MTX), c/o cough + fever + mouth sores.

CC: dry cough x 5d, low grade fever, painful mouth sores x 3d

HPI:
- RA x ~8 yrs, followed by rheum, joints stable lately
- dry cough x 5d, worse at night, no sputum
- fever Tmax 100.8 at home yesterday
- mouth sores x 3d, painful w/ eating
- c/o fatigue + mild DOE x 3d
- denies SOB at rest, hemoptysis, CP, chills
- no new joint swelling, no rash
- no sick contacts at home, no recent travel, no known TB exposure
- appetite down x 3d but drinking fluids OK
- flu + pneumococcal vaccines up to date

Meds per pt:
- MTX 20 mg weekly per pt
- CORRECTION: pharmacy list + pt's bottle reviewed, MTX is 15 mg weekly (6 x 2.5 mg tabs all taken on Sundays), not 20 mg
- folic acid 1 mg daily
- adalimumab 40 mg q2wk, last dose 1 wk ago
- prednisone 5 mg daily
- lisinopril 10 mg daily
- atorvastatin 20 mg daily
- ibuprofen 400 mg PRN joint pain, uses ~3x/wk

Allergy: penicillin (hives as a child)
PMH: RA, HTN, hyperlipidemia
SH: never smoker, no EtOH, works as an accountant, lives w/ wife + 2 kids

Vitals: T 99.9 F, HR 96, BP 132/80, RR 18, SpO2 96% RA at rest, 95% RA w/ ambulation

Exam:
- NAD, speaking full sentences
- oral: 3 shallow ulcers on buccal mucosa, no thrush
- lungs: crackles R base, no wheeze
- CV: RRR, no murmur
- joints: no synovitis, no effusion
- skin: no rash
- eyes: no conjunctivitis
- neck: no LAD
- ext: no edema
- neuro: A&Ox3, nonfocal

Data:
- rapid flu + COVID swabs neg
- CXR: RLL infiltrate, no effusion
- CBC: WBC 5.8, Hgb 12.6, plt 168
- CMP: Cr 0.9, AST 38, ALT 42

Impression:
- RLL pneumonia in pt on MTX + adalimumab + prednisone (immunosuppressed)
- oral mucositis, likely MTX related
- r/o MTX pneumonitis if no response to abx
- RA stable
- HTN, hyperlipidemia stable

Plan:
- start doxycycline 100 mg BID x 7d (penicillin allergy, so no amoxicillin)
- HOLD MTX + adalimumab until pneumonia resolved
- stop ibuprofen (interacts w/ MTX, renal risk) -> acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN
- increase folic acid to 2 mg daily for mucositis
- continue prednisone 5 mg daily, lisinopril, atorvastatin
- salt water rinses QID for mouth sores
- CT chest if not improving in 48-72h
- f/u rheum in 1 wk, PCP in 3d, repeat CXR in 6 wks
- pt counseled on MTX toxicity sx (mouth sores, cough, SOB, fever), call rheum same day if worse
- pt to bring MTX bottle to rheum visit to re-confirm dose
- work note x 3d, rest + fluids
- ED if worsening SOB, SpO2 < 92%, persistent fever
- pt verbalized understanding
summary: A 51-year-old male with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, adalimumab and prednisone presented with 5 days of dry cough, low grade fever and 3 days of painful mouth sores. The methotrexate dose was clarified from the bottle as 15 mg weekly, and he has a penicillin allergy with hives. His temperature was 99.9 F with oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and he had crackles at the right base, shallow oral ulcers, and a right lower lobe infiltrate on chest X-ray. The impression is right lower lobe pneumonia in an immunosuppressed patient with oral mucositis. Doxycycline is started, methotrexate and adalimumab are held, ibuprofen is stopped, and folic acid is increased to 2 mg daily.

soap.subjective: 51-year-old male with rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension and hyperlipidemia on methotrexate, with dry cough for 5 days (worse at night, no sputum), fever to 100.8 at home, painful mouth sores for 3 days, fatigue and mild dyspnea on exertion. Denies shortness of breath at rest, hemoptysis, chest pain, chills, new joint swelling and rash. Medications: methotrexate 15 mg weekly (corrected from the 20 mg first reported), folic acid 1 mg daily, adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks, prednisone 5 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg as needed. Allergy: penicillin (hives as a child). Never smoker.
soap.objective: Temperature 99.9 F, heart rate 96, blood pressure 132/80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 96% on room air at rest and 95% with ambulation. No acute distress, speaking full sentences. Three shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa, no thrush. Crackles at the right base, no wheeze. Regular rhythm without murmur. No synovitis or effusion. No rash. Chest X-ray: right lower lobe infiltrate, no effusion. WBC 5.8, Hgb 12.6, platelets 168. Creatinine 0.9, AST 38, ALT 42.
soap.assessment: Right lower lobe pneumonia in an immunosuppressed patient on methotrexate, adalimumab and prednisone. Oral mucositis, likely methotrexate related. Methotrexate pneumonitis to be ruled out if no response to antibiotics. Rheumatoid arthritis stable. Hypertension and hyperlipidemia stable.
plan: Start doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days (penicillin allergy, so no amoxicillin)
Hold methotrexate and adalimumab until the pneumonia has resolved
Stop ibuprofen (interacts with methotrexate, renal risk); acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed
Increase folic acid to 2 mg daily for mucositis
Continue prednisone 5 mg daily, lisinopril and atorvastatin
Salt water rinses four times daily for mouth sores
CT chest if not improving in 48 to 72 hours
Follow up with rheumatology in 1 week, PCP in 3 days, and repeat chest X-ray in 6 weeks
Go to the ED for worsening shortness of breath, oxygen saturation below 92%, or persistent fever

note:
Dictation for outpatient orthopedic follow-up. The patient is an 85-year-old female seen six weeks after a right total hip arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis. She reports that her pain is much improved, she rates it at 2 out of 10, and she is walking around the house with a walker. She denies fever, chills, calf pain, calf swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, drainage from the incision, or redness around the incision. She had one near fall two weeks ago when the walker caught on a rug but she did not actually fall. She lives alone in a one story home. Her niece lives two hours away and visits on weekends and a neighbor brings groceries, but she has no one at home to help her with bathing, meal preparation, or her medications, and she admits she skips lunch on some days.

Past history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis. Her medications as she reports them are aspirin 81 mg twice daily, which she took for blood clot prevention and finished one week ago, oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed, which she stopped on her own two weeks ago, acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours, amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, and levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, correction, 88 micrograms daily. She also takes vitamin D3 1000 units daily.

On exam today vital signs are blood pressure 134/78, heart rate 76, temperature 98.2, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The posterior incision is well healed with no erythema, no warmth, and no drainage. There is no calf tenderness and no swelling in either leg. Right hip flexion is to 90 degrees, abduction is symmetric, and she is neurovascularly intact distally. Her gait is slow but steady with the walker, with a mild limp.

Imaging today, AP pelvis and lateral right hip x-rays, shows well seated components with no fracture, no lucency, and no loosening. Labs from last week show hemoglobin 10.8, improved from 9.6 at discharge, creatinine 1.2, and hemoglobin A1c 7.1.

Impression is that she is doing well six weeks after a right total hip arthroplasty with healing as expected, mild postoperative anemia that is improving, and a home situation that puts her at risk for falls and missed medications because she lives alone with limited support.

For the plan, weight bearing as tolerated with the walker, and continue posterior hip precautions until the three month visit. The aspirin course is complete, so no further aspirin. Oxycodone is discontinued, and I will change the acetaminophen to 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. Continue her other medications. Order home health physical therapy and occupational therapy and a home safety evaluation, including removal of throw rugs. Refer to social work for in-home support services, home delivered meals, a medical alert device, and pharmacy pill packaging. Recheck hemoglobin in six weeks. Follow up in six weeks with repeat x-rays. She should call for fever, increasing hip pain, redness or drainage at the incision, calf pain, or any fall.
summary: An 85-year-old female returned six weeks after a right total hip arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis with much improved pain, walker use, and one near fall at home. She lives alone with limited support and skips some meals, and she has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism and osteoporosis. The incision is well healed, x-rays show well seated components, and hemoglobin is 10.8 and improving. The impression is expected healing with mild postoperative anemia and fall and medication risks from living alone. Aspirin is finished, oxycodone is discontinued, acetaminophen becomes as needed, and home health therapy, a home safety evaluation, social work, and repeat x-rays in six weeks are arranged.

note:
Hospital day 2 progress note. The patient is a 39-year-old female admitted with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and elevated liver enzymes. She reports that the pain is mild this morning, about 2 out of 10, and she has had mild nausea without vomiting. She denies fever, jaundice, itching, dark urine, and pale stools. She drinks about one glass of wine per month and uses no other substances. Home medications are limited to an over-the-counter turmeric supplement 500 mg daily, which she started three months ago for joint aches, and acetaminophen as needed. She has a documented allergy to codeine, which caused hives.

Overnight there were no events. Vitals this morning: blood pressure 128/78, heart rate 74, temperature 98.2, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Her BMI is 34. On exam she is comfortable and anicteric, the abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and there is no rebound and no guarding. There is no peripheral edema and no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Data: AST 118 and ALT 164 on admission, alkaline phosphatase 112, total bilirubin 0.8, INR 1.0, platelets 245, and hemoglobin 13.1. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.9% and fasting glucose is 131. A right upper quadrant ultrasound shows diffusely increased liver echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis, no gallstones, and a normal common bile duct. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody are negative.

Impression is elevated liver enzymes most consistent with fatty liver disease in the setting of obesity, with newly identified type 2 diabetes. The turmeric supplement may be contributing. Given the codeine allergy, we will avoid opioid analgesics.

Plan is to stop the turmeric supplement and to start metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals. Continue acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, not to exceed 2 grams in 24 hours. Order autoimmune markers, iron studies, and transient elastography before discharge or as an outpatient. Dietitian consult for a weight loss goal of 7 to 10 percent and carbohydrate reduction. Repeat a hepatic panel in two weeks and see her in hepatology clinic in four weeks. We expect discharge tomorrow if her pain remains controlled.

note:
42-year-old male seen in rheumatology clinic for follow-up of fibromyalgia. He was hospitalized for five days about three weeks ago with community-acquired pneumonia and has been home since discharge, having completed his antibiotics. Since coming home he reports a marked increase in widespread muscle pain, worse in the neck, shoulders, and low back, along with poor sleep, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating that he describes as brain fog. He has morning stiffness lasting about 15 minutes. He denies fever, cough, shortness of breath, joint swelling, rash, and dry eyes.

Medications before the admission were duloxetine 30 mg once daily and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. At discharge the hospital team added tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours as needed for pleuritic chest pain, which has since resolved, and he has been taking it about twice a day for his muscle pain. He denies agitation, sweating, and tremor on this combination.

On exam his blood pressure is 124/80, heart rate 78, temperature 98.4, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. His lungs are clear. There is diffuse tenderness over the neck, trapezius, and low back, with no joint swelling, no warmth, and full range of motion of all joints. Strength is normal. The chest x-ray at discharge showed a resolving right lower lobe infiltrate. His TSH last month was 1.9.

My impression is a fibromyalgia flare after the recent hospitalization for community-acquired pneumonia, with disrupted sleep. The pneumonia has clinically resolved. Tramadol is unlikely to help the fibromyalgia pain and adds serotonergic risk on top of duloxetine.

Plan is to increase duloxetine from 30 mg to 60 mg once daily, stop the tramadol, and start cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime for sleep and muscle pain. Continue acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Refer to physical therapy for a graded exercise program and review sleep hygiene. Repeat the chest x-ray six weeks after discharge to confirm the infiltrate has cleared. Follow up in six weeks.

He denies fever, cough, shortness of breath, joint swelling, rash and dry eyes, and exam showed diffuse tenderness without joint swelling. His discharge chest x-ray showed a resolving infiltrate and the pneumonia has clinically resolved. The impression is a fibromyalgia flare after the hospitalization. Duloxetine is increased to 60 mg once daily, tramadol is stopped, cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime is started, physical therapy is arranged and a repeat chest x-ray is planned.

note:
39-year-old female seen in the urology clinic for follow-up of overactive bladder. She reports urinary urgency with frequency of about 12 voids per day, nocturia two to three times per night, and urge incontinence two to three times a week, usually on the way to the bathroom. She tried oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for six weeks, which gave only partial relief and caused troublesome dry mouth and constipation. She denies dysuria, hematuria, fever, and flank pain. She drinks about four cups of coffee per day and little water otherwise. She has no history of kidney stones or pelvic surgery.

She has a documented allergy to sulfa antibiotics, which caused a diffuse rash. She takes no other medicines.

On exam her blood pressure is 126/78 and heart rate 72. The abdomen is soft with no suprapubic tenderness. Urinalysis today shows no blood, no leukocytes, and no nitrites. A bladder scan shows a post-void residual of 25 mL. Her 3-day bladder diary shows an average of 12 voids a day with two to three leaks over the three days.

My impression is overactive bladder with urge incontinence, with a partial response to and poor tolerance of oxybutynin. There is no evidence of infection or incomplete emptying. High caffeine intake is likely contributing.

Plan is to stop oxybutynin because of the side effects and start mirabegron 25 mg once daily, with her blood pressure to be rechecked at the next visit. Behavioral measures include bladder training with timed voiding every 2 to 3 hours, reducing coffee to one cup per day, and limiting fluids in the evening. Refer her for pelvic floor physical therapy. Because of her sulfa allergy, any future urinary infection should be treated with a non-sulfonamide antibiotic. Follow up in 8 weeks with a new bladder diary.

Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 34-year-old male sent over for iron-deficiency anemia. Tell me what led your primary care doctor to check your blood.
Patient: I have been tired for about four months, and I get short of breath on the stairs at work. My wife says I look pale. The blood work showed my iron was very low.
Doctor: Any black or tarry stools?
Patient: No black stools. And no blood when I wipe or in the toilet.
Doctor: Any belly pain, nausea, or vomiting?
Patient: Some burning in the upper stomach, off and on, mostly after meals. No nausea and no vomiting.
Doctor: Any weight loss, trouble swallowing, or change in your bowel habits?
Patient: No weight loss, no trouble swallowing, and my bowels are regular.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Naproxen 500 mg twice a day for my lower back, for about two years. Omeprazole 20 mg once a day for heartburn. Ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice a day for the iron. An albuterol inhaler as needed for asthma. And sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety.
Doctor: Are you really taking the iron twice a day?
Patient: That is what the label says, but honestly I quit the evening pill because it upset my stomach. So it is once a day.
Doctor: Thanks for clarifying, so 325 mg once a day. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Penicillin. I got a bad rash and hives as a kid.
Doctor: Noted, a documented penicillin allergy with hives. Today your blood pressure is 118/70, heart rate 96, temperature 98.3, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. You look pale, with pale inner eyelids and no yellowing of the eyes. Your heart rhythm is regular, your lungs are clear, and your belly is soft with mild tenderness in the epigastrium, no masses, and no enlarged liver. On the rectal exam the stool is brown with no mass, and the stool test for occult blood is positive. Your labs from last month show hemoglobin 9.4, a low MCV of 71, and ferritin 5. The celiac antibody test was negative, but the Helicobacter pylori stool antigen came back positive.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: My impression is iron-deficiency anemia from slow blood loss in the upper stomach, most likely from your naproxen plus a Helicobacter pylori infection, and your sertraline adds a little to the bleeding risk. We still need to look for any other source. Here is the plan. First, stop the naproxen today and use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for your back. Second, increase the omeprazole from 20 mg once a day to 40 mg twice a day. Third, because of your penicillin allergy we will skip amoxicillin. Instead we will treat the infection for 14 days with bismuth subsalicylate 524 mg four times daily, tetracycline 500 mg four times daily, and metronidazole 500 mg three times daily, along with the omeprazole. Fourth, stop the ferrous sulfate because it upsets your stomach and the tetracycline binds iron, and we will arrange an iron infusion instead. Fifth, I am scheduling an upper endoscopy with biopsies and a colonoscopy within the next two weeks. Continue the albuterol and the sertraline. Repeat your hemoglobin and ferritin in four weeks, and come back to see me after the procedures.
Patient: Is there anything I should watch for?
Doctor: Go to the emergency department if you notice black or bloody stools, faint, or have chest pain.
summary: A 34-year-old male was referred for iron-deficiency anemia after four months of fatigue, exertional breathlessness, pallor and upper stomach burning, with no black stools, bleeding, weight loss or trouble swallowing. He has taken naproxen for two years and has a penicillin allergy with hives. Hemoglobin was 9.4 with low ferritin, the stool occult blood test and Helicobacter pylori stool antigen were positive, and the celiac antibody test was negative. The impression is iron-deficiency anemia from upper GI blood loss, most likely from naproxen plus Helicobacter pylori infection. Naproxen and oral iron are stopped, omeprazole is increased, a penicillin-free 14-day regimen is started, an iron infusion is arranged, and endoscopy and colonoscopy are scheduled.

Dictation for outpatient neurology follow-up. The patient is a 41-year-old female with young onset Parkinson's disease, diagnosed three years ago, correction, four years ago, who comes in for routine follow-up. Over the past two months she reports that each dose of her levodopa seems to wear off about an hour before the next one is due, and during that time she gets stiffness and slowness in the right arm and leg and a return of the tremor in her right hand. She also reports lightheadedness when she stands up quickly and ongoing constipation. She denies falls, hallucinations, compulsive gambling, trouble swallowing, and daytime sleepiness. Her mood has been stable and she is still working full time.

Current medications are carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, one tablet three times daily, pramipexole 0.5 mg three times daily, rasagiline 1 mg once daily, and polyethylene glycol 17 grams daily as needed for constipation.

On exam she has mild hypomimia, a resting tremor in the right hand, mild rigidity of the right arm with cogwheeling, and bradykinesia with right finger tapping. Her gait is steady with decreased arm swing on the right, turns are smooth, and the pull test is normal. Strength and sensation are normal. Labs from last month showed hemoglobin 13.4, creatinine 0.8, and TSH 1.8.

My impression is Parkinson's disease with early wearing off motor fluctuations, and mild orthostatic hypotension, most likely related to her dopaminergic medications. For the plan, I will change carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg from three times daily to four times daily, spaced about four hours apart and taken thirty minutes before meals. Continue pramipexole and rasagiline at the current doses. Increase fluids and dietary salt, rise slowly from sitting, and consider compression stockings. Continue polyethylene glycol and add more fiber. Check a vitamin B12 level. Refer to physical therapy and occupational therapy for gait and hand function training. Return to clinic in three months, sooner if falls or hallucinations.

Nephrology consultation.

Reason for consult: Acute rise in creatinine in a kidney transplant recipient.
Requesting service: Hospital medicine.

History of present illness: The patient is a 73-year-old female with a deceased donor kidney transplant six years ago, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes who was admitted three days ago with four days of watery diarrhea, poor oral intake, and lightheadedness. Her baseline creatinine is 1.3. On admission her creatinine was 2.4, and it has improved to 1.9 after intravenous fluids. The diarrhea is now less frequent. She denies fever, dysuria, blood in the urine, pain over the graft, and new leg swelling. She reports no prior rejection episodes and no known drug allergies.

Current medications: Tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily.

Examination: Blood pressure 108/64, heart rate 88, temperature 98.0, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Mucous membranes are dry, the lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft with a nontender graft in the right lower quadrant. There is no peripheral edema.

Data reviewed: Creatinine 2.4 on admission and 1.9 today. Potassium 5.3 and bicarbonate 19. Tacrolimus trough level 14.2 ng/mL, with a goal of 5 to 8. Urinalysis shows trace protein with no blood and no white cells. Transplant ultrasound with Doppler shows normal graft size, no hydronephrosis, and normal resistive indices. BK virus PCR is pending. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile is negative.

Impression: Acute kidney injury in a kidney transplant, most likely from volume depletion due to diarrhea together with an elevated tacrolimus level, since diarrhea increases tacrolimus exposure. Rejection and obstruction are less likely given the ultrasound and urinalysis, although the BK virus result is still pending. Mild hyperkalemia and a low bicarbonate should improve with fluids.

Recommendations:
1. Reduce tacrolimus from 2 mg twice daily to 1.5 mg twice daily and recheck a trough level in 48 hours.
2. Continue mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily and prednisone 5 mg daily. Do not stop the prednisone.
3. Hold amlodipine while she is volume depleted and her blood pressure is 108/64.
4. Continue isotonic saline at 100 mL per hour for 24 hours, then reassess volume status.
5. Avoid NSAIDs, IV contrast, and other nephrotoxins, and dose all medications for her kidney function.
6. Check a basic metabolic panel daily and follow up the BK virus PCR.
7. If creatinine does not return toward baseline in 48 to 72 hours, we will reassess for further rejection work-up. The transplant nephrology team will follow daily.

Doctor: Good to see you again. I have you down as a 26-year-old female here for follow-up of bipolar I disorder. How have the last few weeks been?
Patient: Honestly rough. I work rotating shifts at a distribution center, and last month they moved me to nights. My schedule changes every week, so my sleep has been all over the place.
Doctor: How much are you sleeping?
Patient: Maybe four hours some days, then ten hours on my days off. About a week ago I had three days where I felt really wired, with racing thoughts, talking fast, and spending too much. It settled after I finally slept.
Doctor: Any thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any voices or seeing things that are not there?
Patient: No hallucinations.
Doctor: How about side effects from the lithium, like shaking, diarrhea, vomiting, or being very thirsty?
Patient: A little hand shaking, but no diarrhea, no vomiting, and I am not extra thirsty.
Doctor: Tell me how you take the lithium.
Patient: Lithium 600 mg in the morning and 600 mg at night. With the shift changes I sometimes take the night dose really late or skip it. Probably twice a week.
Doctor: Any other medicines or supplements?
Patient: Just ibuprofen 400 mg now and then for headaches, maybe three times a week. I have an IUD for birth control.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 114/70 and your heart rate is 80. I see a fine tremor in both outstretched hands. Your speech is a normal rate, your mood is up and down by your report, your thoughts are organized, and you do not seem to be responding to anything unseen. Your labs from this week show a lithium level of 0.5 mEq/L, creatinine 0.8, and TSH 2.1. The lithium level is on the low side, which fits with the missed doses.
Patient: Is the wired stretch the bipolar coming back?
Doctor: My impression is bipolar I disorder with a brief hypomanic episode triggered by sleep disruption from your rotating shifts, and a low lithium level from missed doses. Here is the plan. Keep lithium 600 mg twice daily, but tie the doses to your main sleep period, one when you wake up and one twelve hours later, and set phone alarms. Start melatonin 3 mg thirty minutes before your main sleep period. Stop the ibuprofen, because it can raise your lithium level, and use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for headaches instead. We will repeat the lithium level in two weeks, drawn twelve hours after your last dose, and I would like you to keep a sleep log. I will write a letter asking your employer for a more consistent schedule. Let us meet again in four weeks, and call sooner if you stop sleeping, feel wired again, or have any thoughts of hurting yourself.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
summary: A 26-year-old female with bipolar I disorder who works rotating shifts, recently moved to nights, reports erratic sleep and three days of feeling wired with racing thoughts and talking fast about a week ago, and she misses her night lithium dose about twice a week. She denies thoughts of self-harm and hallucinations, has only mild hand shaking, and her lithium level this week was 0.5 mEq/L with normal creatinine and TSH. The impression is bipolar I disorder with a brief hypomanic episode triggered by sleep disruption and missed lithium doses. Lithium 600 mg twice daily continues with doses tied to sleep, melatonin is started, ibuprofen is stopped, and follow-up is in four weeks.
